# Pushing Boundaries

# A Long Late Antiquity

# Samuel Barber Michael Eber Mateusz Fafinski Elisa Iori Sihong Lin Jakob Riemenschneider Anna M. Sitz

This editorial introduction explains the rationale for this journal and its place in the

current research landscape of late antique studies. While this field has “exploded”,

different specialisms and disciplines continue to approach the period through their own

specific lenses. We contend that further conversations across these boundaries and over

a long late antiquity will be key to advancing the field and offers this journal as a home

for these interdisciplinary conversations.

Keywords: Late Antiquity, historiography, editorial

## Introduction

Few fields have exploded like Late Antiquity. What was once a historical

nadir, a definitive break with the culture of the ancient world, is now seen as

a dynamic period of innovation and transformation.1 On the one hand, Alois

Riegl’s Spätantike, originally denoting a stylistic transition in the visual arts,

has swelled to become a nexus of research in History, the History of Art,

Religious Studies, Archaeology, and more.2 On the other, this rapid expansion

has highlighted the interconnectivity of the late antique past along vectors

that transcend traditional (Western) scholarly boundaries. From Christian

missionaries preaching at the Tang court of Chang’an from the seventh century

onwards,3 to migrations of people and plague across the steppe,4 to Kosmas

Indikopleustes’ discussions of commercial links between Persia, Ethiopia, and

Sri Lanka,5 to an eighth-century Central Asian prince adopting the title Frum

Kesar, “Caesar of Rome,”6 Late Antiquity has never been bigger.

At the same time, integrating this ever-growing scope into a coherent

picture has proven challenging. The surge of research, publications, novel

approaches, and new data has meant attaining a bird’s-eye view of the field in

toto is now essentially impossible—a sure sign of its ongoing success. Yet this

growth has not been met with universal approval. Andrea Giardina, for example,

complained that Late Antiquity’s esplosione centered a narrow spectrum

of disciplinary priorities—principally those of social, cultural, and religious

history.7 Consequently, the place of what was once the period’s primary

historical axis, the Western Roman Empire’s fifth-century dissolution, has

become ambiguous, representing to some merely an ephemeral ripple in the

great currents of the historical longue durée.8 Although debate has long moved

on from drawing strict oppositions between “continuity” and “catastrophe,”

old battle lines are still liable to resurface, particularly between practitioners

of different disciplinary assumptions and/or distinct institutional milieux.9

3 Pushing Boundaries

Most recently, scholarship has turned towards integrating scientific analyses—

particularly from the fields of epidemiology, climate science, and genetics—in

order to augment their understanding of the past, yet this has simultaneously

provoked methodological critique and reflection.10 In general, Late Antiquity’s

underlying assumptions as a paradigm, as well as its relationship to present-day

concerns, remain undertheorized.11

It is in this context that we present Essays in Long Late Antiquity. Taking

an actively expansive view of the field, ELLA seeks to push its boundaries—to

further catalyze its “explosion,” one might say—through wide-ranging, interdis­

ciplinary investigations of the dynamic centuries of the first millennium CE. In

what follows, we seek to locate the journal and its objectives within what we

suggest is a unique moment of historiographical flux.

## Liminality and Connection: Geographic, Temporal, and Institutional Perspectives

From its inception, Late Antiquity has been a liminal period, one located at

the crux of an Antiquity-that-was and a medieval world to come. Though Peter

Brown, to name only the most vociferous of its proponents, has urged that it

be considered a discrete historical era in its own right, the perception of Late

Antiquity as transitional—defined less by its own characteristics than by those

of the periods bracketing it—has persisted.12 One finds traces of this paradigm

not only in the traditional centrality of the Roman Mediterranean’s “Decline”

(and putative Fall), but also in revisionist conceptions of “Transformation.”

Both imply movement from one state to another. More recently, the characteri­

zation of the post-classical world as one of crisis (whether political, climatic, or

archaeology, see e.g., Lavan 2003. epidemiological) echoes the idea that Late Antiquity was an era on the edge. As

much as it is true that no historical period can be analysed as an unchanging,

homeostatic system, this approach to the past has placed too much emphasis

on transition being itself characteristic of late antique societies.

This impasse derives in part from a dissonance between traditional

periodizations founded in political history, on the one hand, and the interdisci­

plinary character of the field as now practised, on the other. Nicholas Matheou

has provocatively argued that the “analytical common sense” of Byzantine

Studies is fundamentally “statist”; that is to say, its assumed subject is the

Eastern Roman Empire itself, its fortunes and its failures.13 A similar point

could be made about Late Antiquity, at least for Europe and the Mediterranean

of the Roman Empire, though similar paradigms also emerge when looking

towards Sasanian Persia, early medieval China, or even periods of consoli­

dation and disintegration on the Central Asian steppe.14 The work taking place

under this umbrella, however, has increasingly concentrated less on the fates

of empires and more on the various apparatuses that made their societies

work—on the domestic, local, and regional arrangements of individuals and

groups and their capacities for adaptation, resilience, and independent action.

This development, then, that is so often described as a turn from “Decline and

Fall” towards “Continuity and Transformation” could just as easily be reckoned

as one from an institutional history of the State towards a variegated tapestry

of interwoven communal histories, whether political, civic, religious, ethnic, or

linguistic in nature.

In this light, temporal boundaries calibrated to events, imperial reigns, or

the tenure of dynasties look increasingly malapropos. Garth Fowden’s proposal

of the first millennium CE as a discrete temporal category from the perspective

of religious history might sound conservative, yet it addresses exactly this

issue, namely, the need for categories that meaningfully and concisely group

comparable phenomena, yet remain flexible enough to account for local

difference.15 From a similar perspective, and as indicated in our title, ELLA

adopts an avowedly “long” definition of the period, stretching from roughly

100 to around 800 CE. Our goal is not to precisely categorize what is or is not

characteristic of Late Antiquity between hard and fast boundaries. Rather, it is

to embrace the broad temporal span in which an array of networked societies

emerged across Afro-Eurasia—abruptly, in some places, less so in others—that

were connected directly, through the mobility of people, objects, and ideas,

and also indirectly, in their shared experiences of supraregional and global

phenomena.

Should we speak of a “Global Late Antiquity,” then? Certainly, the dramatic

societal transformations witnessed during these centuries—from the effects of

climatological change to cultural responses to pandemic disease to political

instability and proselytizing religions—did not respect geographic boundaries

and generated comparable, if not identical, responses across various social

and cultural contexts. Despite its good intentions, however, critics have argued

that the Global Turn, especially in Medieval Studies, has imposed European

and Christian chronological constructs on societies with their own distinct

trajectories, yoking them to frameworks of historical time that would be

unrecognizable to subjects living within them.16 Similarly, continuous expansion

risks a kind of oppressive relativism: the construction of comparative models

that flatten the dissimilar historical and cultural circumstances from which local

phenomena emerge.

To be sure, questions of temporal and geographic division go hand in hand:

to create divisions in time is implicitly to create divisions in space.17 Notably,

Fowden’s argument for the first millennium as a coherent historical period is

partly in response to the methodological naiveté of scrutinizing the emergence

of Islam within a Christian- and European-centric temporal and, implicitly,

geographic schema.18 Unlike the Global Middle Ages, however, Late Antiquity’s

disciplinary gaze has not been trained primarily on Europe per se, but rather

the Mediterranean Basin. For this reason, it more readily resists the charge of

Eurocentrism, though this focus nonetheless instantiates its own disciplinary

borders. As Guy Halsall has perceptively argued, “it remains puzzling why it

should be more acceptable or thought less odd to talk of late antique Axum or

late antique Persia than about late antique Ireland or Denmark.”19

been the subjects of sustained critique. One possibility is to conceptualize

Late Antiquity as an era of “small worlds” that were connected by the people,

objects, and ideas that crossed their geographic and temporal boundaries.20

Without a focus rooted in the local and particular, our image of the past loses

resolution: it becomes difficult to grasp and, perhaps, inadvertently falls

victim to totalizing Grand Narratives that squeeze Late Antiquity between

neighboring periodizations, thereby cementing its “transitional” nature. At

the same time, this period saw major shifts across the Afro-Eurasian sphere,

from the rise of religions variously in alliance and in conflict with state power;

to the spread of revolutionary technologies such as paper or stirrups; to new

ideologies of visual display. We thus encourage contributions that consider the

wider late antique world from a comparative or interconnected perspective

alongside focused, specialist investigations. We intend this as an invitation for

closer dialogue across disciplinary borders and for the recognition of parallel

developments—an addition to, rather than a replacement for, local definitions

of historical time. We note here that similar invitations are being extended by

scholars in other fields.21 It is our hope that ELLA will be a forum in which they

might be answered.

It is a testament to Late Antiquity’s vitality that it is uncommonly receptive

to interdisciplinary theoretical and methodological approaches. At the time of

writing, the training to undertake research in the field might embrace (depending

on the national scholarly context) everything from “traditional” methodological

toolsets such as palaeography, stylistic analysis, or philology to postmodern

critical theories, digital humanistic and computational approaches, and scientific

analyses as noted above. The very “inbetweenness” of Late Antiquity has, in

other words, made it a nexus of disciplinary and methodological innovation. Yet

this expansiveness comes at a cost. At a time when the study of premodernity

in general is devalued and dismissed within broader institutional and national

frameworks, the scholar of Late Antiquity may play the role of the “Swiss

army knife” of the premodern curriculum, straddling multiple methodological,

disciplinary, and temporal areas. At the same time, not being easily categorizable

creates obstacles within the bureaucratized, “impact”-oriented attitude of the

neoliberal university—secure positions dedicated to late antique studies remain

few.

There is no easy solution to these challenges, yet we nonetheless wish to

close on a word of hope. In the foregoing, it should be clear that the expanses of

the late antique world, in every sense, have grown immeasurably and continue

to do so. For some, this may serve as a sign of theoretical incoherence. We take

a different view. While the strictures of contemporary higher education seek to

create atomization, to place us within disciplinary or thematic siloes, to study

Late Antiquity is to invest our specialized expertise in a shared project, to

collaborate across imposed boundaries. It is our hope that that solidarity can

serve as the foundation for lasting change.

## The Inaugural Issue

The contributions to our inaugural issue exemplify this approach. Focusing

particularly on questions of temporality and its reification as historical periodi­

zation, all shine new light on inherited paradigms and so demonstrate the

utility of a “long” Late Antiquity for their respective fields.

Luis Josué Salés brings postcolonial theories to bear on the histori­

ography of late antique philosophy. Making the provocative argument that

“Neoplatonism” was a historiographical invention of the nineteenth century,

he uncovers the foundational role played by essentialized binary distinctions—

between “Aristotelianism” and “Platonism,” “East” and “West”—in the scholarly

conceptualization of this philosophical movement. Contrasting modern Western

European approaches to the Neoplatonist scholars Origen, Gregory of Nyssa,

and Maximos the Confessor with largely neglected nineteenth-century Russian

scholarship, he opens a decolonial path for rethinking Late Antiquity beyond

inherited hierarchies and categories.

In a similar fashion, Michael Höckelmann examines the concept of zhonggu

(中古, “Middle Antiquity”) in Chinese historiography. Stretching from the early

third to the tenth or eleventh centuries CE, zhonggu would seem to represent

a rare instance of overlap with Western ideas of historical categorization. As

Höckelmann shows, however, the evolution of the term’s meaning reveals the

active work performed by paradigms of decline, continuity, and tradition in

the past and the present alike. His article thus encourages us to investigate

how such “regimes of historicity” developed over time in our own fields, and

thus to ask deeper questions beyond the applicability of Western paradigms to

non-Western contexts.

From another angle, Alessia Zubani’s paper scrutinizes the nature and

extent of continuities between Sasanian and early Islamic institutions and

ideas of political authority. Centering on an emblematic case, the now-lost

Sasanian royal chronicle known in Arabic as the Kitāb ṣuwar mulūk Banī Sāsān

(“Book of the Portraits of the Sasanian Kings”), Zubani reconstructs aspects of

its content to offer insights into Sasanian manuscript culture and visual history.

Adopting a comparative and interconnected approach to Late Antiquity, her

contribution both highlights characteristics shared with the visual language of

the neighboring Roman Empire and draws attention to the active reinterpre­

tation of Sasanian imperial memory in the early Islamic centuries.

Michael Eber offers the first English translation of the oldest Latin vita

of Marinus (Marina) the Monk, one of a number of late antique saints who

were assigned female at birth, but lived as men in male monasteries. While

the Greek version of this text is well studied, its movements in and through

the Mediterranean Basin have not received sustained attention. The Latin

vita was, judging by the number of extant manuscripts, the most popular

version, yet has not to date been available in any modern language. Eber’s

contribution thus aims to jump-start new research into the Mediterranean

mouvance of monachoparthenia, the hagiographic motif underlying the story

of Marinus.

Finally, Ellen Muehlberger takes three innovative recent books in Early

Christian Studies as a springboard to meditate on the tools at our disposal

to reconstruct the past. Each work shares an investment in recovering the

“lived” beliefs and practices of Christians beyond the “thin census,” in her

words, represented in the textual record. As she notes, such work has access

to no additional evidence from an empirical standpoint, but rather represents

a reorientation towards the sources themselves—the questions we ask, the

methods we apply, the lessons we draw. Although there is no way to definitively

bridge the chasm between textual representation and the subjectivities of

historical actors, Muehlberger suggests that such methods are not inherently

faulty. Rather, they approximate, they draw us closer to an understanding—an

experience that, as she notes, we share with those early Christians who sought

to understand their own history.

## Essays in Long Late Antiquity: A Mission Statement

ELLA sets out to:

• break down traditional borders between fields defined by geography, time,

and methodology

• provide a forum for interdisciplinary exchange and debate

• draw comparative connections between the established spatio-temporal

foci of “Late Antiquity” and other historical, geographic, and cultural

contexts

• create a publishing venue for the essential (yet critically undervalued)

work of textual editing and translation, especially of shorter, overlooked

sources

In sum, the mission of Essays in Long Late Antiquity is to publish research

essays and translations concerning the period between approximately 100

and 800 CE and the broad geographical region spanning Europe, northern and

eastern Africa, the Indian subcontinent, and Asia. We encourage bold contri­

butions, and especially those that reflect upon the state of the field and its

geographic, temporal, and methodological definition. To that end, collaborative

and co-authored essays are especially welcome. We are active supporters of

Open Access publishing and the free exchange of knowledge to all. Ultimately,

our guiding principle is to look at Late Antiquity not merely as a transitional

period, but as a world of its own. We look forward to discovering where the field

might turn next.
